standard_text: Find the prime factorization of whole numbers and write the results using exponents.

progression.narrative:
Prime factorization rests on one idea: every whole number greater than 1 is either prime -- divisible only by 1 and itself -- or it is composite and can be broken down into a product of primes. The standard asks students to find that product and write it compactly with exponents, so the arc must begin with the vocabulary the whole topic depends on. Before a student can factor anything, they have to look at a number and decide whether it is prime or composite, because a composite number is the only kind that factors further, and the classic trap is calling an odd number like 21 or 51 prime without ever testing 3, 5, or 7.

From there the work is a controlled descent. Students take a composite number and pull out one prime factor at a time -- a factor tree or a division ladder -- until every branch ends in a prime, then write the result as a product like 2 x 2 x 2 x 3. Once that product is reliable, exponent notation is just shorthand: repeated primes get collected, so 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 becomes 2^3 x 3, and 72 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 becomes 2^3 x 3^2. Numbers then grow from under 100 into the 100-200 range, which raises the arithmetic load without changing the method. The capstone flips the task around: students analyze a factorization someone else wrote -- supplying a missing exponent, or judging whether a claimed factorization is correct and fully reduced to primes -- which is only possible once the forward procedure is automatic. The through-line we keep naming: keep dividing until every factor is prime, then collect the repeats into exponents, and always multiply back to check.

steps.rationale: The prerequisite the item spec names explicitly: students must understand prime and composite numbers before factoring. Classifying numbers -- and resisting the 'odd means prime' trap -- is the gate to every later step.

The core mechanic: break a composite number into a product of primes (no exponents yet), continuing until no factor can be split. This is the Below-proficiency factorization task and the foundation of the exponent form.
The standard's headline demand: collect repeated primes into exponents so 3 x 3 x 7 becomes 3^2 x 7. This is the Approaching-proficiency move that turns a product into the compact required form.

The At-proficiency task: independently generate the full prime factorization of a number from 100 to 200 using exponents. Larger numbers raise the arithmetic load and demand a reliable division ladder plus a product check.

The Above-proficiency reversal at DOK 1-2: given a factorization with one exponent hidden, determine the exponent that makes the product equal the number. Requires reading exponent form fluently and verifying by multiplying back.

The Above-proficiency DOK 3 synthesis: judge whether a claimed prime factorization is correct and fully reduced, and justify it -- including recognizing that a prime number's factorization is itself. Hand-authored because no engine stem covers this justification task.

skills.name: Recognize whether a whole number is prime or composite

prerequisite_skill.description: Decide whether a whole number is prime (only factors 1 and itself) or composite (has more factors).
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Is 13 prime or composite? What about 15?

skills.i_do_script: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. A composite number has more than two factors, so it can be split into smaller whole-number factors. Watch: 13 is prime because nothing from 2 to 12 divides it evenly. 15 is composite because 3 x 5 = 15. To test a number I try dividing by 2, then 3, then 5, then 7 -- if any divides evenly, it is composite.

canonical_error.pattern: Calls an odd number prime without testing whether 3, 5, or 7 divides it
canonical_error.example: Says 51 is prime, missing that 51 = 3 x 17
canonical_error.why: The student assumes 'odd means prime' and stops after checking divisibility by 2. Odd numbers still have to be checked against 3, 5, 7, and 11 before they can be called prime.

skills.item_template: A whole number under 100. Student states prime or composite. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Is 13 prime or composite?
Is 15 prime or composite?
Is 51 prime or composite?
Is 47 prime or composite?
Is 1 prime or composite?
Is 91 prime or composite?

redirect_script.stop: Did you test 3, 5, and 7, not just 2?
redirect_script.prompt: Odd does not mean prime. Try dividing by 3, then 5, then 7. If any goes in evenly, it is composite. 51 looks prime, but 3 x 17 = 51.
redirect_script.praise: You checked the small primes before deciding -- that's how you spot a hidden factor.

vocabulary.definition: A whole number greater than 1 with exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
A whole number greater than 1 that has more than two factors, so it can be broken into smaller factors.

worked_example_script.text: Write the number 51.
It's odd -- but is it prime? What might divide it?
Add the digits: 5 + 1 = 6, a multiple of 3, so 3 divides 51. 51 = 3 x 17 -- composite.
If a student says 51 is prime, ask 'did you try dividing by 3?'
Your turn: is 47 prime or composite?

skills.name: Recall multiplication facts and use divisibility rules

prerequisite_skill.description: Recall basic multiplication facts and use divisibility rules for 2, 3, 5, and 10.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Name a factor pair for 24. Is 72 divisible by 3?

skills.i_do_script: Factoring quickly depends on knowing multiplication facts and a few divisibility shortcuts. A number is divisible by 2 if it ends in an even digit, by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5, and by 3 if its digits add to a multiple of 3. Watch 72: it is even, so 2 goes in; and 7 + 2 = 9, a multiple of 3, so 3 goes in too. Knowing 8 x 9 = 72 lets me split it instantly.

canonical_error.pattern: Applies the last-digit test to divisibility by 3 instead of adding the digits
canonical_error.example: Says 72 is not divisible by 3 because it does not end in 3, 6, or 9
canonical_error.why: The student uses the last-digit rule (which works for 2, 5, and 10) on 3, where the rule is about the digit SUM. 7 + 2 = 9 is a multiple of 3, so 72 is divisible by 3.

skills.item_template: A divisibility or factor-pair question. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Is 72 divisible by 3?
Name a factor pair for 24.
Is 95 divisible by 5?
What is 8 x 9?
Is 84 divisible by 2?
Is 81 divisible by 3?

redirect_script.stop: For 3, add the digits -- did you?
redirect_script.prompt: The last-digit test is only for 2, 5, and 10. For 3, add the digits and check whether THAT sum is a multiple of 3. For 72: 7 + 2 = 9, so yes.
redirect_script.praise: You used the digit-sum rule for 3 -- that's the right shortcut.

vocabulary.definition: A whole number that divides another evenly, with no remainder.
A quick test that tells you whether one number divides another without doing the full division.

worked_example_script.text: Write the number 72.
Is it divisible by 2? By 3? How can you tell?
It's even, so 2 works. 7 + 2 = 9, a multiple of 3, so 3 works. 72 = 8 x 9.
If a student says 72 isn't divisible by 3 'because it doesn't end in 3,' remind them to add the digits.
Your turn: is 84 divisible by 3?

skills.name: Classify whole numbers as prime or composite
skills.i_do_script: To classify a list, I test each number for factors other than 1 and itself. Watch this set: 2, 21, 47, 73, 76. 2 is prime. 21 = 3 x 7, composite. 47 -- no small prime divides it, prime. 73 -- prime. 76 is even, composite. So the three primes are 2, 47, and 73. The traps are the odd composites like 21 that look prime until you try dividing by 3.

canonical_error.pattern: Selects an odd composite as prime because it was never tested past divisibility by 2
canonical_error.example: Picks 21 as prime, missing 21 = 3 x 7; or calls 51 prime
canonical_error.why: The student equates 'odd' with 'prime' and never checks 3, 5, or 7. Odd composites (21, 51, 57, 91) are the classic distractors -- each needs a divisibility check before it can be called prime.

skills.item_template: A set of numbers under 100 mixing primes and composites. Student selects the primes. Multi-select.

sample_items.stem: Select three prime numbers.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2, 47, 73 are prime. 21 = 3 x 7 and 76 = 2^2 x 19 are composite (76 is even; 21 fails the digit-sum test for 3).

sample_items.stem: Which of these numbers is prime? 51, 53, 55, 57
sample_items.distractor_logic: 53 is prime. 51 = 3 x 17, 55 = 5 x 11, 57 = 3 x 19 are all odd composites.

sample_items.stem: Select the two prime numbers: 15, 17, 19, 21
sample_items.distractor_logic: 17 and 19 are prime. 15 = 3 x 5 and 21 = 3 x 7.

sample_items.stem: Is 91 prime or composite? Justify your answer.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 91 looks prime but 7 x 13 = 91, so it is composite.

redirect_script.stop: Did you try dividing that odd number by 3 and 7?
redirect_script.prompt: Being odd is not enough to be prime. For each number, test 3, then 7. If one divides evenly, it is composite. 21 = 3 x 7, so it is composite, not prime.
redirect_script.praise: You tested the small primes before calling it prime -- that's careful classifying.

vocabulary.definition: A whole number greater than 1 whose only factors are 1 and itself.
A whole number greater than 1 with more than two factors.

worked_example_script.text: Write the set 2, 21, 47, 73, 76.
Test each one: does anything besides 1 and itself divide it?
2, 47, 73 are prime. 21 = 3 x 7 and 76 is even -- both composite. The three primes are 2, 47, 73.
If a student picks 21, ask 'what is 3 x 7?'
Your turn: which of 51, 53, 55 are prime?

practice_problems.stem: Is 7 prime or composite?
Is 9 prime or composite?
Select three prime numbers: 2, 21, 47, 73, 76
practice_problems.notes: Baits picking 21 (= 3 x 7) as prime.

practice_problems.stem: Classify each as prime or composite: 51, 53, 57
practice_problems.notes: Two odd composites flanking a prime.

practice_problems.stem: Priya sorted some numbers. Find and fix her mistake.
shown_work: Priya wrote: '51 is prime because it is odd and doesn't end in 5.'
practice_problems.answer: 51 is composite: 5 + 1 = 6 is a multiple of 3, so 3 divides 51, and 51 = 3 x 17. Being odd is not enough to be prime.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: treating 'odd' as 'prime.'

practice_problems.stem: Is 49 prime or composite? Explain.
practice_problems.notes: A perfect-square composite that looks prime.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why 2 is the only even prime number.
practice_problems.answer: Every other even number has 2 as a factor besides 1 and itself, so it is composite. Only 2 has exactly two factors (1 and 2), so it is the only even prime.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: justify a general fact.

practice_problems.stem: Find the one composite number hiding in this 'all prime' list: 13, 17, 23, 27, 31.
practice_problems.answer: 27 = 3 x 3 x 3 (= 3^3) is the composite; the rest are prime.
practice_problems.notes: Spot the odd composite among primes.

activities.title: Prime or Composite Sort
materials: Card set of whole numbers under 100 (mix of primes and odd composites)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the number cards face up.
2. Sort each card into 'Prime' or 'Composite.'
3. To place a composite, name a factor pair out loud (e.g., '21 = 3 x 7').
4. For any 'Prime' card, say which small primes you tested (2, 3, 5, 7).
5. Debrief: which odd numbers fooled you into thinking they were prime?

activities.title: Odd Isn't Prime
materials: Slip with Priya's '51 is prime' claim
activities.instructions:
1. Read Priya's claim that 51 is prime because it is odd.
2. Add the digits of 51 and test divisibility by 3.
3. Write the factor pair that proves 51 is composite.
4. Write one sentence: why isn't 'odd' the same as 'prime'?

content.worked_problem: Is 51 prime? Priya said yes because it is odd.
content.error_step: Priya stopped after checking divisibility by 2 and never tested 3.
content.why: 5 + 1 = 6 is a multiple of 3, so 3 divides 51: 51 = 3 x 17, composite.

strategy_links.why: Choral response on 'prime or composite?' for a rapid-fire number set builds the automatic recall this skill needs.
The odd-composite trap (21, 51, 57) is a precise, high-frequency error a find-and-fix directly targets.
A number talk on 'how do you know 91 isn't prime?' surfaces divisibility strategies students can share.

questioning_prompts: What are the only two factors a prime number has?
Did you test dividing by 3, 5, and 7 -- not just 2?
This number is odd -- does that make it prime?
What factor pair shows this number is composite?
Which numbers in the list are the tricky odd composites?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student selects an odd composite (like 21 or 51) as prime.
misconception_redirects.say: Being odd is not enough to be prime. For each number, test 3, then 7. If one divides evenly, it is composite. 21 = 3 x 7, so it is composite, not prime.
misconception_redirects.praise: You tested the small primes before calling it prime -- that's careful classifying.

misconception_redirects.say: 1 has only one factor -- itself -- so it is neither prime nor composite. Prime means exactly two factors.
misconception_redirects.praise: You remembered 1 is a special case -- not prime.

quick_checks.look_for: Composite (3 x 19). An answer of 'prime' means the student didn't test divisibility by 3 (5 + 7 = 12).
41 and 53. Including 49 means the student missed 49 = 7^2.

sentence_starters: ___ is prime because its only factors are 1 and ___.
___ is composite because ___ divides it: ___ = ___ x ___.

worked_solution.stem: From the set 3, 33, 41, 57, 89, select all the prime numbers.

steps.annotation: Prime.
Digit sums 6 and 12 are multiples of 3, so both are composite.

steps.math: 41 and 89: no prime up to their square roots divides them
steps.annotation: Both prime.
The composites 33 and 57 were the odd-looking traps.

faded_example.stem: From the set 5, 15, 19, 27, 53, select all the prime numbers.

steps.math: 5 and 19: only factors are 1 and themselves
steps.annotation: Prime.
Composite.
Test 27: what is 2 + 7, and does 3 divide it?
List all the primes in the set.

skills.name: Write the prime factorization of a number without exponents
skills.i_do_script: To factor a number, I break it into a product and keep breaking any composite piece until everything is prime. Watch 42: 42 = 6 x 7, but 6 is composite, so 6 = 2 x 3. Now every factor is prime: 42 = 2 x 3 x 7. I stop only when no factor can be split further, and I write the primes small to large.

canonical_error.pattern: Stops factoring while a composite factor remains, leaving the factorization incomplete
canonical_error.example: Writes 42 = 6 x 7 and stops, leaving 6 (composite) unfactored instead of 2 x 3 x 7
canonical_error.why: The student treats any product as 'factored' without checking that every factor is prime. Factoring is complete only when no factor can be broken down further.

skills.item_template: A composite number under 100 with three or four prime factors. Student writes the prime factorization as a product without exponents. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: What is the prime factorization of 42?
What is the prime factorization of 60?
What is the prime factorization of 66?
What is the prime factorization of 90?

redirect_script.stop: Is every factor you wrote a prime?
redirect_script.prompt: Check each factor: can it be broken down more? 6 isn't prime -- split it into 2 x 3. Keep going until every factor is prime.
redirect_script.praise: You broke it all the way down to primes -- that's a complete factorization.

vocabulary.definition: A number written as a product of only prime numbers.
A diagram that breaks a number into factors, then breaks each composite factor again until every branch is prime.

worked_example_script.text: Write '42 = ?'
Give me any factor pair of 42.
42 = 6 x 7. But 6 isn't prime: 6 = 2 x 3. So 42 = 2 x 3 x 7 -- all primes.
If a student stops at 6 x 7, ask 'is 6 a prime number?'
Your turn: factor 60 all the way down to primes.

practice_problems.stem: Break 12 into primes.
Factor 30 into primes.
Prime factorization of 42?
practice_problems.notes: Baits stopping at 6 x 7.

practice_problems.stem: Prime factorization of 60?
practice_problems.notes: Four factors; the 2 is used twice.

practice_problems.stem: Marco factored 42. Find and fix his mistake.
shown_work: Marco wrote: '42 = 6 x 7, so the prime factorization is 6 x 7.'
practice_problems.answer: 6 is not prime: 6 = 2 x 3. So 42 = 2 x 3 x 7. Marco stopped before every factor was prime.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: stopping with a composite factor still in the product.

practice_problems.stem: Prime factorization of 66?
practice_problems.notes: 11 is prime -- don't try to split it.

practice_problems.stem: Two students factor 90 different ways: one starts 2 x 45, the other starts 9 x 10. Show they finish at the same prime factorization.
practice_problems.answer: 2 x 45 = 2 x (9 x 5) = 2 x 3 x 3 x 5; 9 x 10 = (3 x 3) x (2 x 5) = 2 x 3 x 3 x 5. Same result either way.
practice_problems.notes: Different trees, same primes (uniqueness).

practice_problems.stem: A number's prime factorization is 2 x 2 x 5. What is the number?
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: multiply the primes back.

activities.title: Factor Tree Race
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair draws a number card.
2. Both partners build a factor tree, but starting from DIFFERENT first factor pairs.
3. Circle every prime at the bottom of each branch.
4. Compare: you should reach the same set of primes even though the trees look different.
5. Debrief: how do you know when a branch is finished?

activities.title: Finish the Factoring
activities.instructions:
1. Read Marco's claim that the prime factorization of 42 is 6 x 7.
2. Check each factor -- is it prime?
3. Break down the composite factor and rewrite the full prime factorization.
4. Write the rule for when factoring is finished.

content.worked_problem: Prime factorization of 42. Marco wrote 6 x 7.
content.error_step: Marco stopped while 6 (a composite) was still a factor.
content.why: 6 = 2 x 3, so 42 = 2 x 3 x 7. Factor until every factor is prime.

strategy_links.why: A factor tree is the concrete-to-abstract representation that makes 'keep splitting composites' visible before the rule is abstracted.
Stopping with a composite factor is a precise error a find-and-fix corrects by checking each factor for primeness.
Modeling one tree, then doing one together, then releasing builds the factoring routine step by step.

questioning_prompts: Is every factor you wrote actually prime?
Can any of your factors be broken down further?
What factor pair could you start with?
How do you know when to stop factoring?
Did you get the same primes even starting a different way?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student stops with a composite factor still in the product (e.g., 6 x 7).
misconception_redirects.say: Check each factor: can it be broken down more? 6 isn't prime -- split it into 2 x 3. Keep going until every factor is prime.
misconception_redirects.praise: You broke it all the way down to primes -- that's a complete factorization.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student tries to split a prime like 7 or 11 further.
misconception_redirects.say: 7 and 11 are prime -- they can't be broken down. Stop a branch as soon as it reaches a prime.
misconception_redirects.praise: You recognized a prime and left it alone -- that's the finish line.

quick_checks.look_for: 2 x 3 x 5. A '6 x 5' answer means a composite factor was left in.
2 x 2 x 2 x 3. An '8 x 3' answer means the 8 wasn't broken down.

sentence_starters: I keep breaking down ___ because it is not prime.
___ = ___ x ___ x ___, and every factor is prime.

worked_solution.stem: Write the prime factorization of 84 (no exponents).

steps.annotation: Start with any factor pair.
Break each composite piece into primes.
Every factor is now prime; write them small to large.
Multiply back to confirm.

faded_example.stem: Write the prime factorization of 36 (no exponents).

steps.annotation: Pick a factor pair.
Break down both sixes.
Write all four prime factors in order.
Multiply back to check you get 36.

skills.name: Write a prime factorization using exponents
skills.i_do_script: Once I have the prime factors, I collect repeats into exponents. Watch 63: 63 = 3 x 3 x 7. The 3 appears twice, so I write 3^2, giving 3^2 x 7. And 72 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 2^3 x 3^2. The exponent just counts how many times a prime is used. A prime that appears once, like the 7 in 63, gets no exponent.

canonical_error.pattern: Attaches the exponent to the wrong prime or leaves repeated primes uncollected
canonical_error.example: Writes 63 = 3 x 7^2 (exponent on the wrong base) or 3 x 3 x 7 instead of 3^2 x 7
canonical_error.why: The student either forgets to collect repeated primes into an exponent, or puts the exponent on the wrong base. The exponent must count how many times THAT specific prime appears.

skills.item_template: A composite number under 100 with a repeated prime factor. Student writes or selects the prime factorization using exponents. MC or expression response.

sample_items.stem: What is the prime factorization of 63?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 63 = 3 x 3 x 7 = 3^2 x 7. '3 x 7' drops a factor; '3 x 21' keeps a composite; '3 x 7^2' puts the exponent on the wrong prime.

sample_items.stem: What is the prime factorization of 72?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 72 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 2^3 x 3^2. The distractors swap the exponents, drop 2s, or keep a composite base.

sample_items.stem: Write the prime factorization of 50 using exponents.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 50 = 2 x 5 x 5 = 2 x 5^2; the 5 repeats, not the 2.

sample_items.stem: Write the prime factorization of 48 using exponents.

redirect_script.stop: How many times does that prime actually appear?
redirect_script.prompt: Count each prime separately. 63 = 3 x 3 x 7 -- the 3 is used twice, so 3^2, and the 7 once. The exponent belongs to the prime that repeats.
redirect_script.praise: You counted each prime and put the exponent on the right base -- that's correct exponent form.

vocabulary.definition: A small raised number that tells how many times the base is multiplied by itself; in 3^2 the exponent is 2.
The number being multiplied repeatedly; in 3^2 the base is 3.

worked_example_script.text: Write '63 = 3 x 3 x 7.'
How many times does the 3 appear? How many times the 7?
Three appears twice, so 3^2; seven once, so just 7. 63 = 3^2 x 7.
If a student writes 3 x 7^2, ask 'which number actually repeats?'
Your turn: write 72 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 using exponents.

practice_problems.stem: Write 2 x 2 x 2 using an exponent.
Write 5 x 5 using an exponent.
Prime factorization of 63 with exponents?
practice_problems.notes: Baits 3 x 7^2 (exponent on the wrong base).

practice_problems.stem: Prime factorization of 72 with exponents?
practice_problems.notes: Two different exponents in one answer.

practice_problems.stem: Dev wrote the prime factorization of 45 with exponents. Find and fix his mistake.
practice_problems.answer: The 3 repeats, not the 5: 45 = 3^2 x 5. Dev put the exponent on the wrong prime. Check: 3^2 x 5 = 9 x 5 = 45.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: exponent on the wrong base.

practice_problems.stem: Write the prime factorization of 36 using exponents.
practice_problems.notes: Both primes are squared.

practice_problems.stem: Which is greater, 2^3 x 3 or 2 x 3^3? Find each value and compare.
practice_problems.answer: 2^3 x 3 = 24; 2 x 3^3 = 54. So 2 x 3^3 is greater.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: where the exponent sits changes the value.

practice_problems.stem: A prime factorization is written as 2^3 x 5^2. What number does it equal?
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: expand the exponents and multiply.

activities.title: Collect the Repeats
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out the expanded-form cards (like 2 x 2 x 2 x 3) and the exponent-form cards (like 2^3 x 3).
2. Match each expanded product to its exponent form.
3. For each match, say how many times each prime repeats.
4. Two exponent cards are decoys with no match -- set them aside and say why.
5. Debrief: how do you decide which prime gets an exponent?

activities.title: Right Base, Right Power
activities.instructions:
1. Read Dev's claim that 45 = 3 x 5^2.
2. Write 45 in fully expanded form (3 x 3 x 5).
3. Circle which prime actually repeats.
4. Rewrite the exponent form correctly and check by multiplying.

content.worked_problem: Prime factorization of 45. Dev wrote 3 x 5^2.
content.error_step: Dev put the exponent on the 5, but it is the 3 that repeats.

strategy_links.why: Bridging expanded form (3 x 3 x 7) to exponent form (3^2 x 7) is exactly the representational-to-abstract move CRA supports.
Putting the exponent on the wrong base is a precise, recurring error a find-and-fix corrects.
Choral response on 'how many times does this prime appear?' hard-wires the collect-the-repeats habit.

questioning_prompts: How many times does each prime appear?
Which prime gets the exponent here, and why?
What does the exponent count?
Is 3^2 the same as 3 x 2? Why not?
Can you write your answer both expanded and with exponents?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student attaches the exponent to the wrong prime or leaves repeats uncollected.
misconception_redirects.say: Count each prime separately. 63 = 3 x 3 x 7 -- the 3 is used twice, so 3^2, and the 7 once. The exponent belongs to the prime that repeats.
misconception_redirects.praise: You counted each prime and put the exponent on the right base -- that's correct exponent form.

misconception_redirects.say: 3^2 means 3 x 3 = 9, not 3 x 2. The exponent tells how many 3s are multiplied together.
misconception_redirects.praise: You expanded the exponent as repeated multiplication -- that's what it means.

quick_checks.look_for: 3^2 x 5. A '3 x 5^2' answer puts the exponent on the wrong prime.
8. An answer of 6 means the student multiplied 2 x 3 instead.

sentence_starters: The prime ___ appears ___ times, so I write ___^___.

worked_solution.stem: Write the prime factorization of 200 using exponents.

steps.annotation: Start with a convenient factor pair.
Break each part into primes.
Count how many times each prime appears.
Write each prime with its exponent.

faded_example.stem: Write the prime factorization of 40 using exponents.

steps.annotation: First factor completely into primes.
Count the repeated prime.
Write the 2 with its exponent (the 5 appears once).
Multiply back to check you get 40.

skills.name: Generate the prime factorization of a number from 100 to 200 using exponents
skills.i_do_script: For a bigger number I use a division ladder: divide by the smallest prime that fits, then keep dividing the quotient. Watch 120: 120 / 2 = 60, 60 / 2 = 30, 30 / 2 = 15, 15 / 3 = 5, and 5 is prime. The primes I divided by are 2, 2, 2, 3, 5, so 120 = 2^3 x 3 x 5. A bigger number doesn't change the method -- I just keep dividing until the quotient is prime, then multiply back to check.

canonical_error.pattern: Stops the division ladder early or drops a prime, so the factorization does not multiply back to the number
canonical_error.example: For 120 writes 2^2 x 3 x 5 (= 60), having divided by 2 only twice instead of three times
canonical_error.why: The student loses count of how many times a prime divides, or quits before reaching a prime quotient. Every division must continue until the quotient is prime, and the factorization must multiply back to the original number.

skills.item_template: A whole number from 100 to 200. Student generates the prime factorization using exponents. Numeric/expression response.

sample_items.stem: Find the prime factorization of 120. Write the answer using exponents.
Find the prime factorization of 144. Write the answer using exponents.
Find the prime factorization of 126. Write the answer using exponents.
Find the prime factorization of 175. Write the answer using exponents.

redirect_script.stop: Does your answer multiply back to the number?
redirect_script.prompt: Keep dividing until the quotient is prime, and count every division. Then multiply your primes back -- if you don't get the original number, you dropped one. 120 needs three 2s: 2^3 x 3 x 5.
redirect_script.praise: You divided all the way to a prime and checked the product -- that's a complete factorization.

vocabulary.definition: A method that divides a number by primes one at a time, stacking the quotients until a prime is reached.
A number written as a product of only prime numbers, using exponents for repeats.

worked_example_script.text: Write '120' and set up a division ladder.
What's the smallest prime that divides 120?
If a student writes 2^2 x 3 x 5, ask 'does that multiply back to 120?'
Your turn: find the prime factorization of 144.

practice_problems.stem: 120 / 2 = ? Then divide that by 2 again.
Find the prime factorization of 100 using exponents.
Prime factorization of 120 (exponents)?
practice_problems.notes: Baits 2^2 x 3 x 5 (= 60), one 2 too few.

practice_problems.stem: Prime factorization of 180 (exponents)?
practice_problems.notes: Three distinct primes, two of them squared.

practice_problems.stem: Lena found the prime factorization of 120. Find and fix her mistake.
shown_work: Lena wrote: '120 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 = 2^2 x 3 x 5.'
practice_problems.answer: That product is only 60, not 120. 120 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 = 2^3 x 3 x 5 -- she divided by 2 one time too few. Check: 8 x 3 x 5 = 120.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: stopping the ladder early; the product doesn't match the number.

practice_problems.stem: Prime factorization of 168 (exponents)?
Find the prime factorization of 189, then explain how you know you're finished.
practice_problems.answer: 189 = 3^3 x 7. You're finished because 7 is prime and nothing divides further; check: 27 x 7 = 189.
practice_problems.notes: Odd number -- 2 never divides it, so start at 3.

practice_problems.stem: Two numbers have prime factorizations 2^2 x 3^2 x 5 and 2^3 x 3 x 5. Which is larger, and what are the numbers?
practice_problems.answer: 2^2 x 3^2 x 5 = 180 and 2^3 x 3 x 5 = 120, so the first (180) is larger.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: compare via expanded values.

activities.title: Division Ladder Relay
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a number card between 100 and 200.
2. Build a division ladder: divide by the smallest prime that fits, write the quotient below, repeat.
3. Stop when the quotient is prime; the primes down the side are your factors.
4. Collect repeats into exponents and MULTIPLY BACK to confirm you get the card's number.
5. Debrief: what tells you the ladder is done?

activities.title: Multiply It Back
materials: Slip with Lena's '2^2 x 3 x 5' work
activities.instructions:
1. Read Lena's answer of 2^2 x 3 x 5 for 120.
2. Multiply her factorization out -- what number do you actually get?
3. Redo the division ladder for 120 and count the 2s.
4. Write the corrected factorization and the product check.

content.worked_problem: Prime factorization of 120. Lena wrote 2^2 x 3 x 5.
content.error_step: Lena divided by 2 only twice; 2^2 x 3 x 5 = 60, not 120.
content.why: 120 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 = 2^3 x 3 x 5. Always multiply back to check.

strategy_links.why: Modeling the division ladder, then doing one together, then releasing is the gradual-release routine this multi-step procedure needs.
The dropped-prime error (product doesn't match) is precisely the mistake a multiply-back find-and-fix catches.
Thinking aloud 'keep dividing until the quotient is prime, then check the product' models the self-monitoring the skill requires.

questioning_prompts: What is the smallest prime that divides this number?
Does your factorization multiply back to the original number?
How many times did 2 divide in?
How do you know you've reached the end of the ladder?
Which primes repeat, and what exponents do they get?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student stops the division ladder early, so the product comes out too small.
misconception_redirects.say: Keep dividing until the quotient is prime, and count every division. Then multiply your primes back -- if you don't get the original number, you dropped one. 120 needs three 2s: 2^3 x 3 x 5.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided all the way to a prime and checked the product -- that's a complete factorization.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides by a composite (like 4 or 6) and calls it a prime factor.
misconception_redirects.say: Divide only by primes. If you used 4, split it into 2 x 2. Restart the ladder using the smallest prime.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used only prime divisors -- that keeps the factorization correct.

quick_checks.look_for: 2^2 x 5^2. A '4 x 25' answer means the composite factors weren't reduced.
No -- it equals 60. Recognizing the mismatch shows the product check is working.

worked_solution.stem: Find the prime factorization of 150 using exponents.

steps.annotation: Divide by the smallest prime, 2.
2 won't go into 75; try 3.
Keep dividing until the quotient is prime.
Collect the two 5s into an exponent.

faded_example.stem: Find the prime factorization of 108 using exponents.

steps.annotation: Divide out both 2s.
Divide out the 3s until the quotient is prime.
Count the primes -- two 2s and three 3s -- and write them with exponents.
Multiply back to check you get 108.

skills.name: Find a missing exponent in a given prime factorization
skills.i_do_script: When a factorization is given with one exponent hidden, I work out how many times that prime must divide the number. Watch: 2 x 3 x 5^x = 150. I know 2 x 3 = 6, and 150 / 6 = 25 = 5 x 5, so 5 is used twice: x = 2. I can also just factor 150 myself (2 x 3 x 5^2) and read the exponent off. The exponent counts how many times its prime appears.

canonical_error.pattern: Guesses the missing exponent without checking that the product equals the number
canonical_error.example: For 2 x 3 x 5^x = 150 answers x = 1 (giving 30) instead of x = 2 (giving 150)
canonical_error.why: The student picks an exponent from the look of the expression instead of testing it. The correct exponent is the one that makes the whole product equal the target number.

skills.item_template: A prime factorization of a number 100-200 with one exponent shown as x. Student finds x. MC or numeric.

sample_items.stem: The prime factorization of 150 is 2 x 3 x 5^x = 150. What is the missing exponent x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2 x 3 x 5^2 = 6 x 25 = 150, so x = 2. x = 1 gives only 30.

sample_items.stem: The prime factorization of 120 is 2^x x 3 x 5 = 120. What is the missing exponent x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2^3 x 3 x 5 = 8 x 15 = 120, so x = 3. x = 2 gives only 60.

sample_items.stem: The prime factorization of 144 is 2^x x 3^2 = 144. What is the missing exponent x?
The prime factorization of 108 is 2^2 x 3^x = 108. What is the missing exponent x?

redirect_script.stop: Does that exponent make the product equal the number?
redirect_script.prompt: Test it: substitute your x and multiply. For 2 x 3 x 5^x = 150, try x = 2: 6 x 25 = 150. If the product isn't the number, adjust the exponent.
redirect_script.praise: You checked the exponent by multiplying back to the number -- that's how you verify it.

vocabulary.definition: A raised number telling how many times the base is multiplied by itself.
A number written as a product of only primes, with exponents for repeated primes.

worked_example_script.text: Write '2 x 3 x 5^x = 150.'
What is 2 x 3? What is 150 divided by that?
2 x 3 = 6, and 150 / 6 = 25 = 5 x 5, so 5 is used twice: x = 2.
If a student answers x = 1, ask 'does 2 x 3 x 5 equal 150?'
Your turn: 2^x x 3 x 5 = 120. Find x.

If 2^x = 8, what is x?

practice_problems.notes: x = 2 gives only 60.

shown_work: Omar wrote: 'x = 2, because there are two primes.'
practice_problems.answer: x counts how many 2s, not how many different primes. 200 / 25 = 8 = 2^3, so x = 3. Check: 8 x 25 = 200.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: guessing from the look of the expression without checking the product.

practice_problems.stem: 2^2 x 3^2 x 5^x = 180. Find x, and explain how you checked.
practice_problems.notes: An exponent of 1 -- the 'difficult' band's exponent-of-1 case.

activities.title: Exponent to Number
activities.instructions:
1. Match each prime-factorization expression to the number it equals.
2. For each match, name the exponent you'd hide and what x would be.
3. Two value cards are decoys with no matching expression -- explain why.
4. Debrief: how does multiplying the factors let you check a missing exponent?

activities.title: Check by Multiplying
activities.instructions:
1. Read Omar's claim that x = 2 for 2^x x 5^2 = 200.
2. Divide 200 by 5^2 to isolate the powers of 2.
3. Factor the result into 2s and count them -- that is x.
4. Substitute your x and multiply back to confirm it equals 200.

content.worked_problem: 2^x x 5^2 = 200. Omar wrote x = 2 'because there are two primes.'
content.error_step: Omar counted the number of different primes instead of how many times 2 appears.

strategy_links.why: Guessing an exponent without checking is a precise error a find-and-fix that ends in a product check corrects.
Studying a correct worked solution beside a flawed one trains students to verify a missing exponent by multiplying back.
Think-pair-share on 'how do you know x isn't 1?' pushes students to justify the exponent, not just state it.

questioning_prompts: What does the exponent x count in this expression?
If you substitute your x, does the product equal the number?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student guesses the exponent without checking the product.
misconception_redirects.say: Test it: substitute your x and multiply. For 2 x 3 x 5^x = 150, try x = 2: 6 x 25 = 150. If the product isn't the number, adjust the exponent.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked the exponent by multiplying back to the number -- that's how you verify it.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student counts the number of different primes instead of the repeats of one prime.
misconception_redirects.say: x counts how many times ITS prime appears, not how many different primes there are. Divide out the other primes and factor what's left.
misconception_redirects.praise: You isolated the prime and counted its repeats -- that's the exponent.

quick_checks.look_for: 5 (160 / 5 = 32 = 2^5). A '4' means the student stopped one division early.
2. An answer of 1 gives only 30 -- the product check catches it.

I divided ___ by the known part to get ___, so x = ___.

steps.annotation: Evaluate the part you already know.
Divide the number by the known part to isolate 5^x.
25 is 5 squared, so the exponent is 2.
Multiply back to confirm.

Factor 32 into 2s.
Count the 2s -- that is x.

skills.name: Verify and justify a prime factorization
skills.i_do_script: To check someone's prime factorization I ask two things: does it multiply back to the number, and is every factor actually prime (fully reduced)? Watch two claims for 40: '2 x 4 x 5' multiplies to 40, but 4 isn't prime, so it is NOT a prime factorization -- the correct one is 2^3 x 5. And for a prime like 83, the prime factorization is just 83 itself, because 83's only factors are 1 and 83.

canonical_error.pattern: Accepts a factorization that multiplies to the number without checking that every factor is prime, or factors a prime number
canonical_error.example: Calls 2 x 4 x 5 the prime factorization of 40 (4 is composite); or writes 83 as a product instead of just 83
canonical_error.why: The student verifies only the product, not that the factors are prime and fully reduced. A prime factorization must use ONLY primes, and a prime number's factorization is the number itself.

skills.item_template: A given (possibly flawed) prime factorization, or a prime number. Student judges correctness and justifies. Constructed response. Hand-authored -- no engine stem.

sample_items.stem: Two students wrote the prime factorization of 83. Student A wrote 3 x 2^4 x 5; Student B wrote 83. Who is correct, and why?
sample_items.answer: Student B. 83 is prime -- its only factors are 1 and 83 -- so its prime factorization is 83 itself. Student A treated 83 as composite; 3 x 2^4 x 5 = 240, not even 83.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 83 is prime; the factorization of a prime is the number itself. Student A's product doesn't even equal 83.

sample_items.stem: Is 2 x 4 x 5 the prime factorization of 40? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. It equals 40, but 4 is composite (2 x 2). The prime factorization is 2^3 x 5.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The product is right but 4 isn't prime, so it isn't fully reduced.

sample_items.stem: Maria writes 90 = 2 x 3^2 x 5. Is she correct? Justify.
sample_items.answer: Yes. Every factor is prime and 2 x 9 x 5 = 90.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Correct: all factors are prime and the product checks out.

sample_items.stem: Is 5 x 9 the prime factorization of 45? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. 9 = 3^2 is composite, so it isn't fully reduced. The prime factorization is 3^2 x 5.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 9 must be broken down; the factorization isn't complete.

sample_items.stem: Is 1 x 2 x 3 x 7 an acceptable prime factorization of 42? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No -- 1 is not prime and should never appear in a prime factorization. The correct form is 2 x 3 x 7.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1 is neither prime nor composite, so it doesn't belong in the factorization.

redirect_script.stop: Are all the factors prime, and does it fully reduce?
redirect_script.prompt: Two checks: multiply back to the number AND make sure every factor is prime. If any factor (like 4 or 9) can be split, it isn't done. And a prime number's factorization is just itself.
redirect_script.praise: You checked both the product and that every factor is prime -- that's a real verification.

vocabulary.definition: Give the reasons that show why an answer is correct.
Broken down so that every factor is prime and none can be split further.

worked_example_script.text: Write two claims for 40: '2 x 4 x 5' and '2^3 x 5.'
Both multiply to 40 -- but is every factor prime in each?
4 is composite (2 x 2), so '2 x 4 x 5' isn't a prime factorization. '2^3 x 5' is correct.
If a student accepts 2 x 4 x 5, ask 'can 4 be broken down more?'
Your turn: is 5 x 9 the prime factorization of 45?

practice_problems.stem: Is 4 a prime factor? Why or why not?
What is the prime factorization of the prime number 29?
Is 2 x 4 x 5 the prime factorization of 40? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: No -- 4 is composite. The correct form is 2^3 x 5.
practice_problems.notes: Baits accepting a correct product that hides a composite factor.

practice_problems.stem: Is 90 = 2 x 3^2 x 5 correct? Justify.
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- all factors are prime and 2 x 9 x 5 = 90.
practice_problems.notes: A correct one, to prevent an 'always wrong' bias.

practice_problems.stem: Two students wrote the prime factorization of 83. Find and fix the error.
shown_work: Student B wrote: '83 is prime, so 83 = 83.'
practice_problems.answer: Student B is correct. 83 is prime (only factors 1 and 83), so its prime factorization is 83. Student A wrongly treated 83 as composite; 3 x 2^4 x 5 = 240, not 83.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: factoring a prime number; the product doesn't even match.

practice_problems.stem: Is 5 x 9 the prime factorization of 45? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: No -- 9 = 3^2. The correct form is 3^2 x 5.
practice_problems.notes: Not fully reduced.

practice_problems.stem: Write a WRONG prime factorization of 60 that still multiplies to 60, and explain what makes it wrong.
practice_problems.answer: e.g., 2 x 6 x 5 = 60, but 6 is composite (2 x 3). The correct form is 2^2 x 3 x 5; it is wrong because a factor isn't prime.
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own error (reverse direction).

practice_problems.stem: A student says every number has a different prime factorization. Is that true? Explain with an example.
practice_problems.answer: Each number has exactly ONE prime factorization, and different numbers have different ones. For example, 12 = 2^2 x 3 always -- you can't write 12 using a different set of primes.
practice_problems.notes: Uniqueness of prime factorization.

activities.title: Valid or Not a Prime Factorization
materials: Card set of claimed factorizations (some valid, some with a composite factor or a 1)
activities.instructions:
1. Read each card, which claims a prime factorization for a number.
2. Sort into 'Valid prime factorization' or 'Not valid (or not reduced).'
3. For every 'not valid' card, name the factor that isn't prime (or the 1) and fix it.
4. Confirm every valid card multiplies back to its number.
5. Debrief: what are the two things every valid prime factorization must satisfy?

activities.title: Fully Reduced?
materials: Slip with the '2 x 4 x 5 = 40' claim
activities.instructions:
1. Read the claim that 2 x 4 x 5 is the prime factorization of 40.
2. Multiply it out -- does it equal 40?
3. Check each factor -- is any of them composite?
4. Rewrite the fully reduced prime factorization and justify why yours is complete.

content.worked_problem: Is 2 x 4 x 5 the prime factorization of 40?
content.error_step: The product is 40, but 4 is composite, so the factorization isn't fully reduced.
content.why: 4 = 2 x 2, so 40 = 2^3 x 5. A prime factorization must use only primes.

strategy_links.why: Judging two students' factorizations side by side is exactly the worked-example-plus-error-analysis move this verify-and-justify skill demands.
Spotting the hidden composite factor (4, 9) or the stray 1 is a targeted find-and-fix.
Think-pair-share on 'which student is right and why?' builds the justification the DOK 3 task requires.

questioning_prompts: Does this factorization multiply back to the number?
Is every factor a prime, or can one be split further?
What is the prime factorization of a prime number?
Why doesn't 1 belong in a prime factorization?
How would you convince a classmate this is (or isn't) correct?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student accepts a factorization that multiplies to the number but still contains a composite factor.
misconception_redirects.say: Two checks: multiply back to the number AND make sure every factor is prime. If any factor (like 4 or 9) can be split, it isn't done. And a prime number's factorization is just itself.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked both the product and that every factor is prime -- that's a real verification.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student tries to factor a prime number like 83 into a product.
misconception_redirects.say: 83 is prime -- its only factors are 1 and 83 -- so its prime factorization is just 83.
misconception_redirects.praise: You recognized a prime and wrote it as itself.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4 (generate the prime factorization of a 100-200 number using exponents) -- the At-proficiency computational core. If they pass, move to S5 (find a missing exponent) and S6 (verify and justify a factorization). If they fail, split: S1 checks whether prime vs composite is understood, and S2 checks whether a number can be broken into primes at all. S3 (collecting repeats into exponents) branches off as the notation support check.
